## Company: Converge Information and Communications Technology Solutions, Inc. (CNVRG)
Sector: Services / Information Technology
Converge Information and Communications Technology Solutions, Inc. (CNVRG) was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission on October 17, 2007 primarily to construct, install, maintain and operate in the Philippine information and communications system. In 2008, the Company was granted a congressional franchise under Republic Act No. 9707 with a term of 25 years effective until August 2034. CNVRG commenced fixed broadband internet operations in June 2012.

CNVRG offers fixed broadband internet services to residential and enterprise customers. The Company offers a menu of fiber broadband residential plans - a wide selection from which customers can choose high-speed connectivity products that best suit their household needs. The Company also provides private data network solutions, cloud and colocation services and other connectivity solutions to enterprises of varying sizes, industries and types. In addition, the Company offers add-on products and services such as speed boosts and pay TV.

As of December 2024, CNVRG's primary telecommunications equipment comprises the nationwide fiber network that spans more than 700,000 kilometers throughout the country, including the backbone, distribution network, and last mile connections. CNVRG has also deployed 8.1 million fiber ports throughout the country as of this date.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
Converge ICT is a straightforward business to understand: it builds and operates a nationwide fiber broadband network in the Philippines, selling connectivity to residential households and enterprise customers. The model is capital-intensive but the service itself is essential and recurring — consumers pay monthly for internet the same way they pay for utilities. With over 700,000 kilometers of fiber deployed and 8.1 million ports nationwide, Converge has built the largest pure-play fixed broadband infrastructure in the country. That physical asset base took over a decade and billions of pesos to construct and cannot be replicated cheaply or quickly — which forms the core of its investment case.

The moat is real but contested. Converge's first-mover advantage in underserved areas outside Metro Manila gave it pricing power and subscriber density that PLDT and Globe are now spending aggressively to erode. The 60%+ EBITDA margin is genuinely industry-leading and reflects the operating leverage of a fully built fiber plant. Switching costs are meaningful — once fiber is pulled to a home, customers rarely churn. The prepaid fiber service (Surf2Sawa) grew 86.7% year-on-year through Q1 2026, opening a lower-ARPU but high-volume growth lane that neither incumbent has matched at scale. The enterprise segment is also accelerating at 20%+ annually, diversifying away from residential dependence. The competitive risk is real, but Converge's cost structure and head start remain durable advantages in most of its geographic markets.

Management quality is strong on the fundamentals that matter most. Founders Dennis Anthony Uy and Maria Grace Uy control 66% of the company through ComClark Network — that is serious skin in the game, and the track record since the 2020 IPO has been one of consistent execution: revenue has compounded at 23%+ annually on a 10-year average and the balance sheet remains conservative at 0.32x debt-to-equity. The one flag worth watching is the ₱421M acquisition of ABS-CBN broadcast assets by an affiliated entity (RBU) — Converge insists it is independently managed, but related-party transactions involving founders always warrant scrutiny. Nothing disqualifying, but worth monitoring in future disclosures. The PSEi removal, while negative for stock price (passive fund selling is now in play), says nothing about business quality — it reflects index methodology, not competitive deterioration.

On valuation, the honest Rule #1 assessment is mixed. At ₱10.04, the stock trades at 6.2x earnings and 0.22x PEG, which is cheap by almost any measure — and the calculated sticker price of ₱16.24 implies 62% upside to fair value. But the Rule #1 MOS buy price of ₱8.12 has not been reached; the current price is 23.6% above that threshold. More importantly, the negative FCF growth (-17.2% on a 10-year average) is a genuine disqualifier under strict Rule #1 criteria. Converge is burning cash on capex to build out its network, and while that investment is rational and should eventually convert to free cash flow as the plant matures, it means you are buying a story about future FCF rather than paying for cash being generated today. The franchise also expires in 2034 — not an imminent threat, but a renewal risk worth acknowledging over a 5-10 year hold horizon.

The bottom line is watch, not buy yet. The business is excellent — durable infrastructure, founder-led, with multiple growth vectors still ahead. The price is becoming interesting, especially with PSEi removal likely pushing additional selling pressure that could close the gap to the ₱8.12 MOS entry. But a disciplined Rule #1 investor does not compromise on margin of safety, and the negative FCF trend adds a second reason to wait. Set an alert at ₱8.50 and watch for FCF to inflect positive as capex normalizes — that combination would make CNVRG a compelling buy for a decade-long hold.
